c.tagline: Japan's first great capital, where sacred deer roam free beneath UNESCO temples and the Great Buddha.

taxi.color: varies by company (often green, black, or livery-branded)
taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered with a base fare around ¥500-700 (~$3-4) for the first 1-2km; readily found at both JR Nara and Kintetsu Nara stations, less common to hail on the street elsewhere.

emergency.note: Japan has no single unified emergency number; 110 reaches police and 119 reaches fire and ambulance services.

avoid.reason: The free-roaming deer in Nara Park can nip, headbutt or snatch food and paper — hold bags and tickets securely.

hood_desc: Home to Todai-ji's Great Buddha Hall, Kasuga Taisha, and the free-roaming sacred deer of Nara Park; the essential first stop for temple-hopping, best for first-time visitors who want everything within walking distance.

A beautifully preserved Edo- and Meiji-era merchant quarter of narrow lanes, wooden townhouses, cafes, and craft shops just south of Nara Park; suits travelers who want a boutique, photogenic base with local character.

The modern transport hub around JR Nara Station with department stores, chain hotels, and easy rail access to Kyoto and Osaka; practical for travelers prioritizing transit convenience and reliable business hotels.

A lively shopping street connecting Kintetsu Nara Station to Nara Park, lined with souvenir shops, restaurants, and arcades; good for travelers who want to be steps from both a station and the sights.

A quiet, leafy residential area near Yoshiki-en and Isuien gardens on the eastern edge of Nara Park, home to the historic Nara Hotel; suits travelers wanting a calmer, more local-feeling stay away from the crowds.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan.

transit.hours: Buses and trains run roughly 5:30 AM to midnight; no late-night rail or bus service.
transit.pay: IC cards (ICOCA, Suica, Pasmo, etc.) are widely accepted on buses and trains; cash also works on buses.
transit.note: Central Nara (Nara Park, Naramachi, both stations) is compact and highly walkable; buses are mainly useful for outlying temples like Horyu-ji.

transit.m: JR/Kintetsu limited express with transfer via Osaka or Tsuruhashi (~75-90 min)
Airport limousine bus to Nara (~90 min, limited schedule)

tip.r: Tipping is not practiced in Japan; attempting to tip at restaurants or with taxi drivers is unnecessary and can cause confusion.

landmarks: Tōdai-ji Temple (Great Buddha Hall)
One of the world's largest wooden buildings houses a fifteen-meter bronze Great Buddha, the awe-inspiring centerpiece of eighth-century Nara.
Nara Park (Nara Kōen)
Over a thousand sacred sika deer roam free among lawns and temples, bowing for crackers in Japan's most enchanting city park.
Kasuga Taisha Shrine
A vermilion Shinto shrine deep in a primeval forest, its paths lined by three thousand moss-covered stone and bronze lanterns.
Kōfuku-ji Temple
The Fujiwara clan's great temple beside Sarusawa Pond, whose elegant five-story pagoda has been Nara's skyline symbol for centuries.
Naramachi (Old Merchant Quarter)
A grid of narrow lanes lined with latticed Edo-period townhouses, now sheltering craft shops, sake breweries and atmospheric cafés.
Nigatsu-dō Hall
A hillside sub-temple of Tōdai-ji whose lantern-hung balcony delivers Nara's finest sunset panorama and hosts the fiery Omizutori festival.
Isuien Garden
A masterful Meiji-era strolling garden that borrows Tōdai-ji's gate and Mount Wakakusa into its serene composition of ponds and teahouses.
Mount Wakakusa (Wakakusayama)
A grassy hill rising behind Nara Park, climbed in thirty minutes for sweeping city views and famously set alight each January.
Yakushi-ji Temple
A UNESCO-listed seventh-century temple of symmetrical twin pagodas, its East Pagoda hailed as frozen music of the Hakuhō period.
Heijō Palace Site
The reconstructed vermilion gates and audience halls of Japan's eighth-century imperial capital rise from vast lawns west of downtown.

train.note: Japan is an island nation with no international trains. Nara has two stations about 500 m apart and it matters which you use: Kintetsu Nara is right at the edge of Nara Park and the temples, while JR Nara is further west and a 20-minute walk from Todai-ji. Kintetsu runs from Osaka-Namba in about 40 minutes and from Kyoto in 35-45 minutes by limited express (a small reserved-seat supplement, bookable online), whereas JR's Yamatoji Line from Osaka and Nara Line from Kyoto are covered by the Japan Rail Pass. There is no Shinkansen station in Nara - come via Kyoto or Shin-Osaka.

bus.note: No international buses exist from Japan. Nara Kotsu (https://www.narakotsu.co.jp/) runs the overnight 'Yamato-go' highway bus between Nara and Tokyo Shinjuku, plus the premium Dream Sleeper service and a daytime express to Nagoya; Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) sells comparable overnight seats in English. Highway buses stop at both JR Nara and Kintetsu Nara stations. Direct limousine buses also link Nara with Kansai International Airport (about 1.5 hours) and Osaka Itami, which is usually easier than dragging luggage through two train changes.

ferry.note: Nara is landlocked in the Nara Basin with no navigable river or lake service, so there are no ferries; the nearest passenger ports are in Osaka and Kobe, about two hours away.

half.blurb: A temple complex in Ikaruga housing the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the world, dating to the 7th century.

half.name: Asuka
half.blurb: Japan's ancient capital region, dotted with stone burial mounds and the ruins of 6th-century imperial palaces.

half.name: Yoshino
half.blurb: A mountain famous for thousands of cherry trees planted in tiers, centered on the Kinpusen-ji temple complex.

half.name: Osaka
half.blurb: A major port city with Osaka Castle, the Dotonbori canal district, and dense street-food alleys.

half.name: Kyoto
half.blurb: Japan's former imperial capital, with thousands of temples and shrines including Fushimi Inari and Kinkaku-ji.
